content: An updated Cochrane Review served as the evidence base for evaluating cervical priming methods prior to vacuum aspiration. This review included 61 studies, with 8 new studies added. Approximately half of these studies contributed to the development of the Evidence-to-Decision (EtD) framework, which assessed various cervical priming methods, including natural or synthetic osmotic dilators. For pregnancies under 12–14 weeks, misoprostol or mifepristone is suggested as cervical priming agents before surgical abortion. Studies comparing misoprostol and mifepristone showed that misoprostol resulted in a shorter procedure time, while mifepristone achieved greater pre-procedure cervical dilation. Both medications had comparable side-effect profiles, though the evidence for side effects was of very low certainty. For consistency, the gestational age cut-off for recommendations was set at 12 weeks, though evidence included pregnancies up to 14 weeks. For surgical abortions at 12 weeks or later, cervical priming is recommended. Between 12 and 19 weeks, medication alone (preferably a combination of mifepristone and misoprostol) or a combination of medication and osmotic dilators is suggested. When osmotic dilators are used, the interval between placement and the procedure should not exceed two days. For abortions at 19 weeks or later, a combination of osmotic dilators and medication is recommended. Limited evidence exists for cervical priming in pregnancies between 12 and 14 weeks, so clinical judgment should guide the choice of method in this range. The use of mifepristone combined with misoprostol is preferred over misoprostol alone due to higher cervical dilation and shorter procedure times. Similarly, combining medication with laminaria is favored over laminaria alone, as it results in greater cervical dilation, reduced need for further dilation, and shorter procedure times. These findings are supported by high-certainty evidence, particularly for higher gestational ages. Cervical priming beyond 12–14 weeks can be self-managed, potentially reducing travel and staff time. Community health workers (CHWs) and pharmacy workers have been recommended to provide medical abortion for pregnancies under 12 weeks, as this requires similar skills to those needed for cervical priming. Pharmacists can dispense medications for cervical priming as part of the surgical abortion process, ensuring continuity of care. Evidence supports the safety and effectiveness of nurses, midwives, and auxiliary nurse midwives (ANMs) in providing cervical priming and manual vacuum aspiration (MVA). The gestational age for cervical priming recommendations was amended from beyond 12 weeks to 12 weeks and above to align with updated guidelines. The expert panel emphasized the importance of ensuring continuity of care during the interval between cervical priming and the surgical procedure, with access to health systems for additional support if needed. Key human rights considerations include ensuring non-discrimination and equitable access to cervical priming as part of abortion care. Restrictions on which health workers can provide abortion care often limit access and are inconsistent with WHO guidance. Expanding the range of health workers authorized to provide abortion care improves timely access, reduces costs, and prevents unsafe self-managed abortions. Conscientious objection by health workers can delay access to abortion care and increase abortion-related morbidity and mortality. The WHO recommends against provider restrictions that are inconsistent with its guidance. States must also regulate conscientious objection to reflect best clinical practices and protect abortion seekers' rights.
